title: Solutions in the Environment

competencies.text: Explain characteristics of solutions in household products, industry, and environmental science.
Investigate salt's effect on plant growth.

days.title: What Is a Solution?
days.content:
🎯 Learning Target

This week you will explain the characteristics of solutions in household products, industry and the environment, and investigate how salt affects plant growth.

💧 Solute + Solvent = Solution

A solution is a homogeneous mixture: the particles are spread evenly, so it looks the same throughout. The solute is what dissolves (usually the smaller amount); the solvent does the dissolving (usually the larger amount).

TypeExample
Solid in liquidSalt in water, sugar in coffee
Gas in liquidCO₂ in softdrinks, O₂ in river water
Liquid in liquidVinegar (acetic acid in water), rubbing alcohol
Gas in gasAir (oxygen, CO₂ and others in nitrogen)
Solid in solidAlloys such as brass and stainless steel

🔍 Properties

  • Particles are too small to see and do not settle.
  • They pass through filter paper — you cannot filter salt out of seawater.
  • They can be separated by evaporation or distillation.

Water is called the universal solvent because its polar molecules can pull apart many substances.

✅ Quick Check

3 questions — read each explanation.

scenario.text: In a glass of sweetened iced tea, what is the solvent?

choices.label: Water
Sugar
Tea leaves
Ice cubes only

scenario.explanation: Water is present in the largest amount and dissolves the sugar and tea flavor.

scenario.text: Muddy river water is cloudy and the mud settles to the bottom. Is it a solution?

choices.label: No — its particles settle out, so it is not uniform
Yes — any mixture that contains water is a solution
Yes — mud dissolves completely in river water
No — solutions must always be colored liquids

scenario.explanation: Solutions are homogeneous and do not settle. Muddy water is a suspension; its particles separate over time.

scenario.text: Why can't you remove salt from seawater with filter paper?

choices.label: Dissolved particles pass through the filter
Salt sticks to the filter paper and blocks it
Filter paper adds more salt to the water
Seawater is too cold to pass through paper

scenario.explanation: Dissolved salt is broken into tiny particles that go through filter pores. Evaporation or distillation is needed.

days.title: Concentration and Solubility
days.content:
📏 Concentration

Concentration tells how much solute is in a given amount of solution. A dilute solution has little solute; a concentrated one has a lot. Labels often give concentration as a percentage — for example, 70% isopropyl alcohol or 5% acetic acid in vinegar.

% by volume = (volume of solute ÷ volume of solution) × 100

Example: 30 mL of alcohol in 100 mL of solution is 30% alcohol.

🧂 Saturation

  • Unsaturated — more solute can still dissolve.
  • Saturated — no more solute dissolves at that temperature; extra settles at the bottom.
  • Supersaturated — more solute than normal, made by cooling a hot saturated solution slowly; it crystallizes easily.

🌡️ What Affects Solubility?

Most solids dissolve better in hotter water — sugar dissolves faster and more in hot coffee. Gases are the opposite: they dissolve better in cold water and under pressure. That is why a warm softdrink goes flat quickly and why warm river water holds less oxygen for fish.

🔗 Activity 1 — Match the Pairs

Match each term to its meaning. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

match.why: Usually present in the smaller amount.

match.right: The substance that does the dissolving
match.why: Water is the most common solvent.
Weak juice is a dilute solution.

match.right: Has a large amount of solute
match.why: Strong brine for tuyo is concentrated.
Extra sugar settles at the bottom.
CO₂ is kept dissolved by pressure.
An alloy of copper and zinc.
Warm rivers hold less oxygen for fish.

days.title: Solutions at Home, in Industry and in Nature
days.content:
🏠 Household Products

Vinegar, rubbing alcohol, bleach, mouthwash, oral rehydration salts (ORS) and softdrinks are all solutions. Following the label's dilution instructions matters: too strong can harm skin or surfaces; too weak may not work. ORS must be mixed with the exact amount of water so the body can absorb it properly.

🏭 Industry

  • Electroplating uses metal-salt solutions to coat objects.
  • Fish sauce (patis) and bagoong use concentrated salt solutions to preserve fish.
  • Factories use solvents to clean, extract and mix products — and must treat wastewater before release.

🌊 The Environment

Rivers and seas are natural solutions carrying dissolved oxygen, minerals and salts. Problems arise when the balance changes:

  • Thermal pollution: hot wastewater lowers dissolved oxygen, stressing fish.
  • Saltwater intrusion: over-pumping coastal wells lets seawater seep into freshwater aquifers, making wells salty.
  • Acid rain: gases from burning fuels dissolve in rainwater, forming weak acids.

🎯 Activity 2 — Scenario Challenge

Apply solution concepts to real situations. Read every explanation. You need 70%; retakes are unlimited.

scenario.text: A bottle of softdrink is left open in the sun and goes flat faster than one kept in the refrigerator. Why?

choices.label: Gases dissolve less in warm liquids
Sunlight turns CO₂ into sugar inside
Cold drinks have more water than warm
Warm liquids dissolve more of any gas

scenario.explanation: Gas solubility drops as temperature rises, so CO₂ escapes faster from the warm drink.

scenario.text: A factory releases hot (but clean) water into a river, and fish begin to die. What is the MOST likely cause?

choices.label: The hot water holds less dissolved oxygen
The hot water contains dissolved poisons
Fish cannot swim in river water that is moving
Heat makes the river water much saltier

scenario.explanation: Warm water holds less oxygen. This thermal pollution can suffocate fish even without toxic chemicals.

scenario.text: A mother mixes an ORS sachet with half the water the label says. What is the problem?

choices.label: Too concentrated — it can worsen dehydration
Too dilute — it will not taste salty enough
No problem — stronger ORS works faster
No problem — the amount of water never matters

scenario.explanation: Overly concentrated ORS can pull water into the gut instead of helping absorption. The label's dilution must be followed.

scenario.text: You keep stirring sugar into iced tea, but some sugar stays at the bottom no matter how long you stir. The tea is now…

choices.label: Saturated at that temperature
Unsaturated and needs more sugar
Diluted by the melting ice cubes
Turned into a suspension of tea leaves

scenario.explanation: When no more solute dissolves at a given temperature, the solution is saturated; extra solute settles.

scenario.text: A coastal town pumps its wells heavily, and the well water begins tasting salty. What is happening?

choices.label: Seawater is seeping into the freshwater aquifer
Rain is carrying salt from the air into the wells
The pipes are dissolving into salty minerals
Fish are adding salt to the groundwater supply

scenario.explanation: Over-pumping lowers fresh groundwater, letting denser seawater move inland underground — saltwater intrusion.

days.title: Investigating Salt and Plant Growth
days.content:
🌱 Why Salt Harms Plants

Roots absorb water by osmosis — water moves across a membrane from where there is more water (less solute) to where there is less water (more solute). When the soil water is very salty, water can move out of the roots instead of in. The plant wilts and its leaves turn yellow even if the soil looks wet. This is osmotic stress.

🧪 A Fair-Test Investigation

PartIn this experiment
QuestionHow does salt concentration affect mung bean (monggo) growth?
Independent variableSalt concentration: 0%, 1%, 2%, 4%
Dependent variableSeedling height after 7 days
Controlled variablesSame seeds, soil, cup size, light, amount of water
Control group0% (plain water)

Use several seeds per group and average the results. A typical finding: growth decreases as salt concentration increases. This explains why farms hit by storm surges or saltwater intrusion lose crops, and why researchers breed salt-tolerant rice.

🔐 Formative Check — Escape the Lab

3 lives, 6 keys. You need 70% (5 of 6). Read each explanation.

choices.label: A uniform mixture of solute and solvent
Any mixture whose parts settle out
A single pure substance with no separate parts
A mixture that can be filtered apart

escape.explanation: A solution is homogeneous — evenly mixed, with particles that do not settle or filter out.

escape.text: Which of these is a GAS-in-LIQUID solution?

choices.label: Carbonated softdrink
Brass doorknob (an alloy)
Salt water
Rubbing alcohol

escape.explanation: A softdrink has CO₂ gas dissolved in water. Brass is solid-in-solid; salt water is solid-in-liquid; alcohol is liquid-in-liquid.

escape.text: In the salt-and-monggo experiment, what is the INDEPENDENT variable?

choices.label: Salt concentration of the water
Height of the seedlings after a week
Type of cup used for every group
Amount of sunlight each cup receives

escape.explanation: The independent variable is what the experimenter changes on purpose. Height is measured (dependent); cups and light are controlled.

escape.text: Why does very salty soil make a plant wilt?

choices.label: Water moves out of the roots by osmosis
Salt blocks sunlight from reaching leaves
Salt makes the roots grow much too fast
Salt adds too much oxygen to the soil

escape.explanation: With more solute outside the roots, water moves out of root cells, so the plant cannot take in enough water.

escape.text: A rubbing-alcohol bottle says 70% isopropyl alcohol. In 500 mL, how much is alcohol?

choices.label: 350 mL
70 mL
150 mL
430 mL

escape.explanation: 70% of 500 mL = 0.70 × 500 = 350 mL of alcohol; the rest is mostly water.

escape.text: Why is the 0% salt group needed in the experiment?

choices.label: It is the control for comparing results
It makes the plants grow taller in all cups
It reduces the total cost of the experiment
It is the group expected to die the fastest

escape.explanation: The control shows normal growth without salt, so you can tell whether salt caused any difference.
